4.1 Convergent sequences

Definition 29
#

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.limit

For a sequence \((x_n)\) in a metric space and \(p \in X\),

\[ x_n \to p \iff \forall \varepsilon {\gt} 0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n \ge N,\ d(x_n,p){\lt}\varepsilon . \]

The blueprint also uses the bundled predicates “\((x_n)\) is convergent” and “\(\lim x_n\)”.

Theorem 30
#

Uses

  • Definition 29
  • Definition 18

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.convergesTo_iff_eventually_in_ball

For a sequence \((x_n)\) and \(p \in X\),

\[ x_n \to p \iff \forall r{\gt}0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n \ge N,\ x_n \in B(p,r). \]
Proof ▶

This is just a reformulation of the definition of convergence: the inequality \(d(x_n,p){\lt}r\) says exactly that \(x_n\) belongs to the open ball \(B(p,r)\).

Theorem 31
#

Uses

  • Theorem 30

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.limit_unique

Limits of sequences in metric spaces are unique.

Proof ▶

Assume \(x_n o p\) and \(x_n o q\). If \(p eq q\), let \(\varepsilon = frac12 d(p,q){\gt}0\). Eventually the sequence lies in both \(B(p,\varepsilon )\) and \(B(q,\varepsilon )\). For such an index \(n\), the triangle inequality gives \(d(p,q)\le d(p,x_n)+d(x_n,q){\lt}\varepsilon +\varepsilon =d(p,q)\), a contradiction.

Theorem 32
#

Uses

  • Definition 29
  • Definition 19

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.convergent_isBounded
\[ x_n \to p \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (x_n)\text{ is bounded}. \]
Proof ▶

Choose \(N\) so that \(n\ge N\) implies \(x_n\in B(p,1)\). The finitely many initial terms \(x_0,\dots ,x_{N-1}\) are bounded as well, so taking a radius large enough to contain them together with \(B(p,1)\) shows that the whole sequence is bounded.

Theorem 33
#

Uses

  • Definition 19
  • Definition 29

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.sequence_of_limitPoint

If \(p\) is a limit point of \(E\), then there exists a sequence \((x_n)\) such that

\[ \forall n,\ x_n \in E,\qquad x_n \ne p,\qquad x_n \to p. \]
Proof ▶

Because \(p\) is a limit point, each deleted ball \(B^\ast (p,1/(n+1))\) meets \(E\). Choose \(x_n\in E\cap B^\ast (p,1/(n+1))\). Then \(x_n eq p\) and \(d(x_n,p){\lt}1/(n+1)\), which tends to \(0\). Hence \(x_n o p\).

Theorem 34
#

Uses

  • Definition 29
  • Theorem 31

Lean declarations

  • ConvergentSequences.cnv_mul

For complex-valued sequences,

\[ x_n \to x,\ y_n \to y \Longrightarrow x_n+y_n \to x+y,\quad x_ny_n \to xy, \]
\[ x_n \to x,\ c \in \mathbb {C} \Longrightarrow cx_n \to cx,\quad x_n+c \to x+c. \]
Proof ▶

These are the usual \(\varepsilon \)–\(N\) estimates. For sums and scalar translates, one splits the error using the triangle inequality. For products, write \(x_ny_n-xy=x_n(y_n-y)+y(x_n-x)\) or an equivalent decomposition; convergence gives control of each term, and boundedness of convergent sequences keeps the remaining factors under control.
